arXiv:0806.4084v1 [math.AP] 25 Jun 2008

Existence and uniqueness results for the Boussinesq system with data in Lorentz spaces

Raphaël Danchin Note: Université Paris-Est, LAMA UMR 8050, 61 av. du Général de Gaulle, 94010 Créteil Cedex, France. E-mail: danchin$@$univ-paris12.fr    Marius Paicu Note: Université Paris-Sud, Laboratoire de Mathématiques, Bâtiment 425, 91405 Orsay Cedex, France.
Abstract

This paper is devoted to the study of the Cauchy problem for the Boussinesq system with partial viscosity in dimension N≥3.N\geq 3. First we prove a global existence result for data in Lorentz spaces satisfying a smallness condition which is at the scaling of the equations. Second, we get a uniqueness result in Besov spaces with negative indices of regularity (despite the fact that there is no smoothing effect on the temperature). The proof relies on a priori estimates with loss of regularity for the nonstationary Stokes system with convection. As a corollary, we obtain a global existence and uniqueness result for small data in Lorentz spaces.

MSC: 35Q35, 76N10, 35B65, 76D99

Key words: Boussinesq system, lorentz spaces, critical spaces, losing estimates.

1 Introduction and main results

The present paper is devoted to the mathematical study of the so-called Boussinesq system with partial viscosity:

{∂tθ+u⋅∇θ=0∂tu+u⋅∇u−ν​Δ​u+∇Π=θ​eNdiv​u=0.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\theta+u\cdot\nabla\theta=0\\ \partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u-\nu\Delta u+\nabla\Pi=\theta\,e_{N}\\ \,\mbox{div}\,u=0.\end{cases} (1)

Above, θ=θ⁡(t,x)\theta=\theta(t,x) and Π=Π⁡(t,x)\Pi=\Pi(t,x) are real valued functions, and u=u⁡(t,x)u=u(t,x) is a time dependent vector field. We denote by eNe_{N} the vertical unit vector of ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}. It is assumed that the space variable xx belongs to ℝN.\mathbb{R}^{N}. We supplement the system with Cauchy conditions (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) at time t=0t=0 and address the question of solvability for t≥0t\geq 0.

Boussinesq system arises in simplified models for geophysics in which case uu stands for the velocity field and the forcing term θ​eN\theta\,e_{N} is proportional either to the temperature, or to the salinity or to the density (see [17]). Here, we shall call θ\theta the temperature.

Remark that the standard incompressible Navier-Stokes equations arise as a particular case of (1) (just take θ≡0\theta\equiv 0). Hence, it is tempting to study whether the classical theory for the Navier-Stokes equations may be extended to those more general fluids. As far as one is concerned with global results, the main difficulty that we have to face is that θ\theta is transported by the flow of u.u. Hence it has no time decay nor gain of smoothness whatsoever and the standard approach for solving Navier-Stokes equations with a (given) source term is bound to fail. Nevertheless, in a recent paper (see [11]), we have stated that system (1) has global finite energy weak solutions for any data (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) in L2L^{2} and that uniqueness holds true in dimension two. That result may be compared with Leray’s theorem [16] for the Navier-Stokes equations.

In [11], we have also obtained a global existence result (for small data) in the spirit of Fujita and Kato’s theorem (see [12] and [14]) for the Navier-Stokes equations:

Theorem 1

Let N≥3.N\geq 3. Let θ0∈LN3​(ℝN)∩B˙N,10​(ℝN)\theta_{0}\in L^{\frac{N}{3}}(\mathbb{R}^{N})\cap\dot{B}^{0}_{N,1}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) and u0∈LN,∞​(ℝN)∩B˙p,1−1+Np​(ℝN)u_{0}\in L^{N,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{N})\cap\dot{B}^{-1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,1}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) for some p∈[N,∞].p\in[N,\infty]. There exists a positive cc depending only on NN and such that if

‖u0‖LN,∞+ν−1​‖θ0‖LN3≤c​ν\|u_{0}\|_{L^{N,\infty}}+\nu^{-1}\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{\frac{N}{3}}}\leq c\nu

then Boussinesq system (1) admits a unique global solution

(θ,u,∇Π)∈𝒞⁡(ℝ+,B˙N,10)×(𝒞⁡(ℝ+,B˙p,1Np−1)∩Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,B˙p,1Np+1))N×(Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,B˙p,1Np−1))N.(\theta,u,\nabla\Pi)\in{\cal C}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\dot{B}^{0}_{N,1})\times\Bigl({\cal C}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\dot{B}^{\frac{N}{p}-1}_{p,1})\cap L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\dot{B}^{\frac{N}{p}+1}_{p,1})\Bigr)^{N}\times\Bigl(L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\dot{B}^{\frac{N}{p}-1}_{p,1})\Bigr)^{N}.

Besides, from dimension N=4N=4 on, space LN3​(ℝN)L^{\frac{N}{3}}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) may be replaced by LN3,∞​(ℝN).L^{\frac{N}{3},\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{N}).

The reader is referred to section 2 for the definition of Lorentz spaces Lp,∞L^{p,\infty} and Besov spaces B˙p,rs\dot{B}^{s}_{p,r} which have been used above. Remind that we have the (continuous) inclusions

B˙N,10⊂LN⊂LN,∞.\dot{B}^{0}_{N,1}\subset L^{N}\subset L^{N,\infty}.

Theorem 1 may be interpreted in terms of scaling of Boussinesq system. Indeed, (1) is obviously invariant under the transform

u⁡(t,x)⟼λ​u​(λ2​t,λ​x)andθ⁡(t,x)⟼λ3​θ​(λ2​t,λ​x)for allλ>0.u(t,x)\longmapsto\lambda u(\lambda^{2}t,\lambda x)\quad\text{and}\quad\theta(t,x)\longmapsto\lambda^{3}\theta(\lambda^{2}t,\lambda x)\quad\hbox{for all}\ \ \lambda>0.

Hence data (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) belong to a functional space EE which is at the scaling of the system if and only if the norm of EE is invariant by

u0​(x)⟼λ​u0​(λ​x)andθ0​(x)⟼λ3​θ0​(λ​x).u_{0}(x)\longmapsto\lambda u_{0}(\lambda x)\quad\text{and}\quad\theta_{0}(x)\longmapsto\lambda^{3}\theta_{0}(\lambda x). (2)

In dimension N≥3,N\geq 3, the spaces LN3×(LN,∞)NL^{\frac{N}{3}}\times\bigl(L^{N,\infty}\bigr)^{N} and LN3,∞×(LN,∞)NL^{\frac{N}{3},\infty}\times\bigl(L^{N,\infty}\bigr)^{N} satisfy (2). Hence, Theorem 1 is a global well-posedness result for suitably smooth data satisfying a scaling invariant smallness condition. In fact, prescribing additional regularity in homogeneous Besov spaces ensures that the velocity belongs to the set Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,Lip)L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\hbox{Lip}) of locally integrable functions in tt with values in the set of Lipschitz vector fields. This property was needed for uniqueness. Note in passing that the additional condition required for the initial velocity still satisfies (2).

The present paper aims at weakening as much as possible the Besov space assumption. Ideally, we would like to consider general (small) data (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) in the scaling invariant space LN3,∞×(LN,∞)N.L^{\frac{N}{3},\infty}\times\bigl(L^{N,\infty}\bigr)^{N}.

For proving existence, the strategy is the following. We smooth out the data so that Theorem 1 provides a sequence (θn,un)(\theta^{n},u^{n}) of global solutions which is bounded in

L∞​(ℝ+,LN3,∞×(LN,∞)N).L^{\infty}\bigl(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{\frac{N}{3},\infty}\times\bigl(L^{N,\infty}\bigr)^{N}\bigr).

Obviously, those bounds are insufficient to pass to the limit in the nonlinear terms. However, the parabolicity of the second equation of (1) provides additional regularity so that there is some chance to pass to the limit anyway provided θ0\theta_{0} belongs also to Lp,∞L^{p,\infty} for some large enough p.p. Those basic considerations will enable us to prove the following statement:

Theorem 2

Let u0u_{0} be a solenoidal vector field with coefficients in LN,∞.L^{N,\infty}. Assume that θ0\theta_{0} belongs to

  • •

    L1∩Lp,∞L^{1}\cap L^{p,\infty} for some p>3/2p>3/2 if N=3,N=3,

  • •

    L4/3,∞∩Lp,∞L^{4/3,\infty}\cap L^{p,\infty} for some p>4/3p>4/3 if N=4,N=4,

  • •

    LN/3,∞∩Lp,∞L^{N/3,\infty}\cap L^{p,\infty} for some p≥N/3p\geq N/3 if N≥5.N\geq 5.

There exists a constant c>0c>0 depending only on N,N, and such that if

‖u0‖L3,∞+‖θ0‖L1≤c​νifN=3,‖u0‖LN,∞+‖θ0‖LN/3,∞≤c​νifN≥4\|u_{0}\|_{L^{3,\infty}}+\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{1}}\leq c\nu\ \ \hbox{if}\ \ N=3,\qquad\|u_{0}\|_{L^{N,\infty}}+\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{N/3,\infty}}\leq c\nu\ \ \hbox{if}\ \ N\geq 4 (3)

then system (1) has a global solution (θ,u,∇Π)(\theta,u,\nabla\Pi) with u∈L∞​(ℝ+,LN,∞)u\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{N,\infty}) and

θ∈L∞​(ℝ+,L1∩Lp,∞)ifN=3,θ∈L∞​(ℝ+,LN3,∞∩Lp,∞)ifN≥4.\theta\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{1}\cap L^{p,\infty})\ \ \hbox{if}\ \ N=3,\qquad\theta\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{\frac{N}{3},\infty}\cap L^{p,\infty})\ \ \hbox{if}\ \ N\geq 4.

Remark: In fact, the heat semi-group supplies some additional regularity properties for uu (that we shall use in the proof of Theorem 2).

Note that from dimension 55 on, one can take p=N/3p=N/3 so that the above statement is a global existence result in a scaling invariant space for the system. The scaling of the system may still be almost achieved in dimension 4.4. In dimension 33 however, it is very unlikely that an existence result may be proved for θ0∈L1\theta_{0}\in L^{1} and u0∈LN,∞u_{0}\in L^{N,\infty} (see Remark 4 for further explanations).

As regards uniqueness, let us stress that for general u0u_{0} in LN,∞L^{N,\infty} the function et​Δ​u0e^{t\Delta}u_{0} (where (et​Δ)t>0(e^{t\Delta})_{t>0} denotes the heat semi-group) need not be in Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,Lip).L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\hbox{Lip}). Therefore, the velocity field of the solution constructed in Theorem 2 need not be in Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,Lip)L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\hbox{Lip}) either which precludes us from proving stability estimates for system (1) by mean of standard arguments. Indeed, we have to deal with a transport equation associated to a vector field which is not in Ll​o​c1​(ℝ+,Lip).L^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\hbox{Lip}). This difficulty has been overcome in [11] in the framework of two-dimensional finite energy solutions. In the present paper, we shall see that similar arguments may be used to state uniqueness in dimension N≥3.N\geq 3.

Theorem 3

Let (θ1,u1,∇Π1)(\theta_{1},u_{1},\nabla\Pi_{1}) and (θ2,u2,∇Π2)(\theta_{2},u_{2},\nabla\Pi_{2}) satisfy (1) with the same data. Assume that for some p∈[1,2N[p\in[1,2N[ and i=1,2,i=1,2, we have

θi∈LT∞​(B˙p,∞−1+Np)​and​ui∈LT∞​(B˙p,∞−1+Np)∩L~T1​(B˙p,∞1+Np).\theta_{i}\in L^{\infty}_{T}(\dot{B}^{-1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty})\quad\!\!\text{and}\quad\!\!u_{i}\in L_{T}^{\infty}(\dot{B}^{-1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty})\cap\widetilde{L}_{T}^{1}(\dot{B}^{1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty}).

There exists a constant c>0c>0 depending only on NN and on pp such that if in addition

‖u1‖L~T1​(B˙p,∞1+Np)+ν−1​‖u2‖LT∞​(B˙p,∞−1+Np)≤c\|u_{1}\|_{\widetilde{L}_{T}^{1}(\dot{B}^{1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty})}+\nu^{-1}\|u_{2}\|_{L_{T}^{\infty}(\dot{B}^{-1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty})}\leq c (4)

then (θ1,u1,∇Π1)≡(θ2,u2,∇Π2)(\theta_{1},u_{1},\nabla\Pi_{1})\equiv(\theta_{2},u_{2},\nabla\Pi_{2}).

In the above statement, the space L~T1​(B˙p,∞1+Np)\widetilde{L}_{T}^{1}(\dot{B}^{1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty}) is slightly larger than the set LT1​(B˙p,∞1+Np)L^{1}_{T}(\dot{B}^{1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty}) of integrable functions over [0,T][0,T] with values in the Besov space B˙p,∞1+Np\dot{B}^{1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty} (see section 2).

Remark: The limit case p=2​Np=2N may be considered if the velocity field belongs to a Besov space with third index 11 (see Theorem 5).

Finally, putting together the embedding LN,∞↪B˙q,∞−1+NqL^{N,\infty}\hookrightarrow\dot{B}^{-1+\frac{N}{q}}_{q,\infty} for q>Nq>N (see Lemma 2 below), the existence and uniqueness theorems, and the further regularity properties for the velocity given by the heat semi-group, one ends up with the following global well-posedness result:

Theorem 4

Assume that (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) satisfies the assumptions of Theorem 2 with p=N.p=N. Then system (1) has a unique solution (θ,u,∇Π)(\theta,u,\nabla\Pi) such that u∈L∞​(ℝ+,LN,∞),u\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{N,\infty}), θ∈L∞​(ℝ+,LN3,∞)\theta\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{\frac{N}{3},\infty}) if N≥4N\geq 4 and θ∈L1​(ℝ+,L1)\theta\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{1}) if N=3N=3, with moreover

u∈L~l​o​c1​(B˙q,∞1+Nq)for allq>N.u\in\widetilde{L}^{1}_{loc}(\dot{B}^{1+\frac{N}{q}}_{q,\infty})\quad\hbox{for all}\ \ q>N.

The paper is structured as follows. In the next section, we present a few tools borrowed from harmonic and functional analysis. Section 3 is devoted to the proof of existence. The study of uniqueness is postponed in section 4.

2 Tools and functional spaces

2.1 Lorentz spaces

To start with, let us recall the definition of weak LpL^{p} spaces (denoted by Lp,∞L^{p,\infty}):

Definition 1

For 1≤p<∞,1\leq p<\infty, we denote by Lp,∞​(ℝN)L^{p,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) (or simply Lp,∞L^{p,\infty}) the space of all real valued measurable functions over ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} such that

∥f∥Lp,∞:=supλ>0λ|{x∈ℝN/|f(x)|>λ}|1p<∞.\|f\|_{L^{p,\infty}}:=\sup_{\lambda>0}\lambda\>\Bigl|\bigl\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}/|f(x)|>\lambda\bigr\}\Bigr|^{\frac{1}{p}}<\infty.
Remark 1

The space Lp,∞L^{p,\infty} may be alternatively defined by real interpolation:

Lp,∞=(L∞,L1)(1p,∞).L^{p,\infty}=(L^{\infty},L^{1})_{(\frac{1}{p},\infty)}.

In other words, a function ff belongs to Lp,∞L^{p,\infty} if and only if, for all A>0A>0, one may write f=fA+fAf=f^{A}+f_{A} for some functions fA∈L1f_{A}\in L^{1} and fAf^{A} in L∞L^{\infty} such that

∥fA∥L1≤CA1−1/pand∥fA∥L∞≤CA−1/p.\|f_{A}\|_{L^{1}}\leq CA^{1-1/p}\quad\hbox{and}\quad\|f^{A}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq CA^{-1/p}.

The “best constant” CC defines a norm which is equivalent to ‖f‖Lp,∞.\|f\|_{L^{p,\infty}}.

The set 𝒞c∞{\cal C}_{c}^{\infty} of smooth compactly supported functions is not dense in spaces Lp,∞.L^{p,\infty}. It turns out however that 𝒞c∞{\cal C}_{c}^{\infty} is locally dense in Lp,∞L^{p,\infty} (despite the fact that Lp,∞L^{p,\infty} is not separable). More details are given in the following proposition.

Proposition 1

For all p∈]1,∞[p\!\in]1,\infty[ and f∈Lp,∞,f\in L^{p,\infty}, there exists a family (fε)ε>0(f_{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon>0} of 𝒞c∞{\cal C}_{c}^{\infty} functions and a constant CC so that

supε>0‖fε‖Lp,∞≤C​‖f‖Lp,∞andfε→finL1+L∞.\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\|f_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{p,\infty}}\leq C\|f\|_{L^{p,\infty}}\quad\hbox{and}\quad f_{\varepsilon}\rightarrow f\quad\hbox{in}\ \ L^{1}+L^{\infty}. (5)

Proof:  Let (φε)ε>0(\varphi_{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon>0} be a family of mollifiers and (χε)ε>0,(\chi_{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon>0}, a family of cut-off functions with values in [0,1],[0,1], supported in B⁡(0,2​ε−1)B(0,2\varepsilon^{-1}) and equal to 11 in a neighborhood of B⁡(0,ε−1).B(0,\varepsilon^{-1}).

Let f∈Lp,∞.f\in L^{p,\infty}. For all ε>0,\varepsilon>0, set fε:=φε⋆(χε​f)f_{\varepsilon}:=\varphi_{\varepsilon}\star(\chi_{\varepsilon}f) and fix some η>0.\eta>0. From the above definition and remark, it is obvious that

‖fε‖Lp,∞≤C​‖χε​f‖Lp,∞≤C​‖f‖Lp,∞for allε>0,\|f_{\varepsilon}\|_{L^{p,\infty}}\leq C\|\chi_{\varepsilon}f\|_{L^{p,\infty}}\leq C\|f\|_{L^{p,\infty}}\quad\hbox{for all}\quad\varepsilon>0,

and that one can find two functions g∈L1g\in L^{1} and h∈L∞h\in L^{\infty} such that f=g+hf=g+h and ‖h‖L∞≤η/4\|h\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\eta/4 (just take AA large enough).

Let us split fε−ff_{\varepsilon}-f as follows:

fε−f={φε⋆(χε​g)−φε⋆g}+{φε⋆g−g}+{φε⋆(χε​h)−h}.f_{\varepsilon}-f=\Bigl\{\varphi_{\varepsilon}\star\bigl(\chi_{\varepsilon}g\bigr)-\varphi_{\varepsilon}\star g\Bigr\}+\Bigl\{\varphi_{\varepsilon}\star g-g\Bigr\}+\Bigl\{\varphi_{\varepsilon}\star\bigl(\chi_{\varepsilon}h\bigr)-h\Bigr\}.

On the one hand, Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem and standard results on convolution ensure that the first two terms between curly brackets have L1L^{1} norm less than η/2\eta/2 for small enough ε.\varepsilon. On the other hand, the L∞L^{\infty} norm of the last term is obviously less than η/2\eta/2 for any ε>0.\varepsilon>0.

It is now easy to complete the proof of the proposition.  

2.2 Besov spaces

In this subsection we define the Littlewood-Paley decomposition and the Besov spaces that we are going to work with. The reader is referred to the monographs [5], [15] or [18] for a more detailed presentation.

To start with, fix a smooth nonnegative radial function χ\chi with support in the ball {|ξ|≤43},\{|\xi|\leq\frac{4}{3}\}, value 11 over {|ξ|≤34},\{|\xi|\leq\frac{3}{4}\}, and such that r↦χ⁡(r​er)r\mapsto\chi(re_{r}) be nonincreasing over ℝ+.\mathbb{R}_{+}. Let φ⁡(ξ)=χ⁡(ξ/2)−χ⁡(ξ).\varphi(\xi)=\chi(\xi/2)-\chi(\xi). We obviously have

∑q∈ℤφ⁡(2−q​ξ)=1for allξ∈ℝN∖{0}.\sum_{q\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\varphi(2^{-q}\xi)=1\quad\hbox{for all}\quad\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{N}\setminus\{0\}. (6)

We define the spectral localization operators Δ˙q\dot{\Delta}_{q} and S˙q\dot{S}_{q} (q∈ℤq\in{\mathbb{Z}}) by

Δ˙q​u:=φ⁡(2−q​D)​uandS˙q​u:=χ⁡(2−q​D)​u.\dot{\Delta}_{q}\;u:=\varphi(2^{-q}D)u\quad\text{and}\quad\dot{S}_{q}\,u:=\chi(2^{-q}D)u.

For any tempered distribution u∈𝒮′​(ℝN)u\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{N}), functions Δ˙q​u\dot{\Delta}_{q}u and S˙q​u\dot{S}_{q}u are analytic with at most polynomial growth and u=∑q∈ℤΔ˙q​u\displaystyle{u=\sum_{q\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\dot{\Delta}_{q}u} modulo polynomials (see e.g. [15]).

We shall often use the following quasi-orthogonality property :

Δ˙k​Δ˙q​u≡0if|k−q|≥2andΔ˙k​(S˙q−1​u​Δ˙q​v)≡0if|k−q|≥5.\dot{\Delta}_{k}\dot{\Delta}_{q}u\equiv 0\quad\mbox{if}\quad|k-q|\geq 2\quad\mbox{and}\quad\dot{\Delta}_{k}(\dot{S}_{q-1}u\dot{\Delta}_{q}v)\equiv 0\quad\mbox{if}\quad|k-q|\geq 5. (7)

Let us now recall the definition of homogeneous Besov spaces.

Definition 2

Let s∈ℝ,(p,r)∈[1,∞]2s\in\mathbb{R},\,(p,r)\in[1,\infty]^{2} and u∈𝒮′​(ℝN).u\in{\cal{S}}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{N}). We set

‖u‖B˙p,rs:=(∑q∈ℤ2r​q​s​‖Δ˙q​u‖Lpr)1rifr<∞,and​‖u‖B˙p,∞s:=supq∈ℤ 2q​s​‖Δ˙q​u‖Lp.\|u\|_{\dot{B}^{s}_{p,r}}:=\Big(\sum_{q\in{\mathbb{Z}}}2^{rqs}\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}\,u\|_{L^{p}}^{r}\Big)^{\frac{1}{r}}\quad\text{if}\quad r<\infty,\quad\text{and}\!\quad\|u\|_{\dot{B}^{s}_{p,\infty}}:=\sup_{q\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\,2^{qs}\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}\,u\|_{L^{p}}.

    If s<Nps<\frac{N}{p} or s=Nps=\frac{N}{p} and r=1r=1 then the homogeneous Besov space B˙p,rs:=B˙p,rs​(ℝN)\dot{B}^{s}_{p,r}:=\dot{B}^{s}_{p,r}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) is defined as the set of those tempered distributions uu such that ‖u‖B˙p,rs<∞.\|u\|_{\dot{B}^{s}_{p,r}}<\infty.

  • •

    If Np+k≤s<Np+k+1\frac{N}{p}+k\leq s<\frac{N}{p}+k+1 (or s=Np+k+1s=\frac{N}{p}+k+1 and r=1r=1) for some k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} then B˙p,rs\dot{B}^{s}_{p,r} is the set of tempered distributions uu so that ∂αu∈B˙p,rs−k−1\partial^{\alpha}u\in\dot{B}^{s-k-1}_{p,r} for all multi-index α\alpha of length k+1.k+1.

‖u‖Bp,rs<∞with‖u‖Bp,rs:=‖S˙0​u‖Lp+‖2q​s​‖Δ˙q​u‖Lp‖ℓr​(ℕ).\|u\|_{B^{s}_{p,r}}<\infty\quad\hbox{with}\quad\|u\|_{B^{s}_{p,r}}:=\|\dot{S}_{0}u\|_{L^{p}}+\bigl\|2^{qs}\|\dot{\Delta}_{q}u\|_{L^{p}}\bigr\|_{\ell^{r}(\mathbb{N})}.

The following Bernstein inequality will be of constant use in the paper.

Lemma 1

Let k∈ℕ,k\in\mathbb{N}, 1≤p1≤p2≤∞1\leq p_{1}\leq p_{2}\leq\infty and ψ∈𝒞c∞​(ℝN).\psi\in{\cal C}_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{N}). There exists a constant CC depending only on k,k, NN and Supp​ψ{\rm Supp}\,\psi such that

‖Dk​ψ​(2−q​D)​u‖Lp2≤C​2q⁡(k+N⁡(1p1−1p2))​‖ψ⁡(2−q​D)​u‖Lp1.\hskip 28.45274pt\|D^{k}\psi(2^{-q}D)u\|_{L^{p_{2}}}\leq C2^{q\bigl(k+N\bigl(\frac{1}{p_{1}}-\frac{1}{p_{2}}\bigr)\bigr)}\|\psi(2^{-q}D)u\|_{L^{p_{1}}}.

We shall also use the following fundamental properties of Besov spaces.

Proposition 2

(i) The set B˙p,rs​(ℝN)\dot{B}^{s}_{p,r}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) is a complete subspace of 𝒮′​(ℝN){\cal S}^{\prime}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) if and only if s<N/ps<N/p or s=N/ps=N/p and r=1.r=1.

c−1​‖u‖B˙p,rs≤‖∇u‖B˙p,rs−1≤c​‖u‖B˙p,rs.c^{-1}\|u\|_{\dot{B}^{s}_{p,r}}\leq\|\nabla u\|_{\dot{B}^{s-1}_{p,r}}\leq c\|u\|_{\dot{B}^{s}_{p,r}}. (8)

We shall often use the fact that Lorentz spaces are embedded in Besov spaces (see the proof in [11]).

Lemma 2

For any 1<p<q≤∞,1<p<q\leq\infty, we have

Lp,∞​(ℝN)↪B˙q,∞Nq−Np​(ℝN).L^{p,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{N})\hookrightarrow\dot{B}^{\frac{N}{q}-\frac{N}{p}}_{q,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{N}).

In order to pass to the limit in the nonlinear terms of System (1), the following compactness result in nonhomogeneous Besov spaces will be most useful.

Lemma 3

For any 1<p<q≤∞,1<p<q\leq\infty, ε>0\varepsilon>0 and ψ∈𝒞c∞,\psi\in{\cal C}_{c}^{\infty}, the map u↦ψ​uu\mapsto\psi u is compact from Lp,∞​(ℝN)L^{p,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{N}) to Bq,∞Nq−Np−ε​(ℝN).B^{\frac{N}{q}-\frac{N}{p}-\varepsilon}_{q,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{N}).

2.3 Product and paraproduct in Besov spaces

In order to bound the nonlinear terms in system (1), it will be useful to know how the product of two functions operates in Besov spaces. In fact, optimal results may be achieved by taking advantage of (basic) paradifferential calculus, a tool which was introduced by J.-M. Bony in [4]. More precisely, the product of two functions ff and gg may be decomposed according to

f​g=T˙f​g+T˙g​f+R˙​(f,g)fg=\dot{T}_{f}g+\dot{T}_{g}f+\dot{R}(f,g) (9)

where the paraproduct operator T˙\dot{T} is defined by the formula

T˙f​g:=∑qS˙q−1​f​Δ˙q​g,\displaystyle{\,\dot{T}_{f}g:=\sum_{q}\dot{S}_{q\!-\!1}f\,\dot{\Delta}_{q}g},

and the remainder operator, R˙,\dot{R}, by

R˙​(f,g):=∑qΔ˙q​f​Δ~q​gwithΔ~q:=Δ˙q−1+Δ˙q+Δ˙q+1.\displaystyle{\,\dot{R}(f,g):=\sum_{q}\dot{\Delta}_{q}f\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}g}\quad\text{with}\quad\widetilde{\Delta}_{q}:=\dot{\Delta}_{q\!-\!1}+\dot{\Delta}_{q}+\dot{\Delta}_{q\!+\!1}.

We shall make an extensive use of the following results of continuity for operators T˙\dot{T} and R˙\dot{R} (see the proof in e.g. [18]):

Proposition 3

Let 1≤p,p1,p2,r,r1,r2≤∞1\leq p,p_{1},p_{2},r,r_{1},r_{2}\leq\infty so that 1p=1p1+1p2\frac{1}{p}=\frac{1}{p_{1}}+\frac{1}{p_{2}} and 1r=1r1+1r2.\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1}{r_{1}}+\frac{1}{r_{2}}.

  • •

    from L∞×B˙p,rtL^{\infty}\times\dot{B}^{t}_{p,r} to B˙p,rt\dot{B}^{t}_{p,r} for all t∈ℝ,t\in\mathbb{R},

    from B˙p1,r1−s×B˙p2,r2t\dot{B}^{-s}_{p_{1},r_{1}}\times\dot{B}^{t}_{p_{2},r_{2}} to B˙p,rt−s\dot{B}^{t-s}_{p,r} for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} and s>0.s>0.

Operator R˙\dot{R} is continuous:

  • •

    from B˙p1,r1s×B˙p2,r2t\dot{B}^{s}_{p_{1},r_{1}}\times\dot{B}^{t}_{p_{2},r_{2}} to B˙p,rs+t\dot{B}^{s+t}_{p,r} for all (s,t)∈ℝ2(s,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{2} such that s+t>0,s+t>0,

    from B˙p1,r1s×B˙p2,r2−s\dot{B}^{s}_{p_{1},r_{1}}\times\dot{B}^{-s}_{p_{2},r_{2}} to B˙p,∞0\dot{B}^{0}_{p,\infty} if s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R} and 1r1+1r2≥1.\frac{1}{r_{1}}+\frac{1}{r_{2}}\geq 1.

{∂tu−νΔu+∇Π=f,divu=0,u|t=0=u0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}u-\nu\Delta u+\nabla\Pi=f,\qquad{\rm div}\,u=0,\\ u_{|t=0}=u_{0},\end{array}\right. (17)

3 Existence of solutions with infinite energy

This section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 2. The principle of the proof is standard:

  1. 1.

    approximate the data (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) by a sequence (θ0n,u0n)n∈ℕ(\theta_{0}^{n},u_{0}^{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} of smooth solutions;

  2. 2.

    solve (globally) the Boussinesq system with data (θ0n,u0n);(\theta_{0}^{n},u_{0}^{n});

  3. 3.

    resort to compactness arguments to prove the convergence of a subsequence;

  4. 4.

    pass to the limit in the system.

3.1 Global existence: the smooth case

As a warm up, let us first consider the case p=Np=N which is easier to deal with. For notational simplicity, we agree that LN3,∞L^{\frac{N}{3},\infty} stands for L1L^{1} if N=3.N=3.

Let (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) be in (LN3,∞∩LN,∞)×(LN,∞)N\bigl(L^{\frac{N}{3},\infty}\cap L^{N,\infty}\bigr)\times\bigl(L^{N,\infty}\bigr)^{N} with div​u0=0.\,\mbox{div}\,u_{0}=0. According to (a slight generalization of) Proposition 1, one can find a sequence (θ0n,u0n)n∈ℕ(\theta_{0}^{n},u_{0}^{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} of 𝒞c∞{\cal C}_{c}^{\infty} functions which tends to (θ0,u0)(\theta_{0},u_{0}) in the sense of the distributions and such that in addition

‖θ0n‖LN3,∞≤C​‖θ0‖LN3,∞,‖θ0n‖LN,∞≤C​‖θ0‖LN,∞,‖u0n‖LN,∞≤C​‖u0‖LN,∞.\|\theta_{0}^{n}\|_{L^{\frac{N}{3},\infty}}\leq C\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{\frac{N}{3},\infty}},\quad\|\theta_{0}^{n}\|_{L^{N,\infty}}\leq C\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{N,\infty}},\quad\|u_{0}^{n}\|_{L^{N,\infty}}\leq C\|u_{0}\|_{L^{N,\infty}}.

Note that projecting on the set of solenoidal vector fields is needed to ensure that div​u0n=0.\,\mbox{div}\,u_{0}^{n}=0. This operation is harmless since 𝒫{\cal P} maps LN,∞L^{N,\infty} in LN,∞.L^{N,\infty}.

According to [11] Theorem 1.5, we deduce that there exists a positive constant cc so that if condition (3) is satisfied then system (1) admits a unique global solution (θn,un)(\theta^{n},u^{n}) in 𝒞⁡(ℝ+,B˙N,10){\cal C}(\mathbb{R}_{+};\dot{B}^{0}_{N,1}) with in addition

‖un​(t)‖LN,∞≤C⁡(ν−1​‖θ0‖LN3,∞+‖u0‖LN,∞)for allt≥0.\|u^{n}(t)\|_{L^{N,\infty}}\leq C(\nu^{-1}\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{\frac{N}{3},\infty}}+\|u_{0}\|_{L^{N,\infty}})\quad\hbox{for all}\ \ t\geq 0.

As θ0∈LN3,∞∩LN,∞\theta_{0}\in L^{\frac{N}{3},\infty}\cap L^{N,\infty} and div​un=0\,\mbox{div}\,u^{n}=0 one can assert (see e.g Proposition 4.6 of [11]) that

‖θn​(t)‖LN3,∞≤C​‖θ0‖LN3,∞and‖θn​(t)‖LN,∞≤C​‖θ0‖LN,∞for allt≥0.\|\theta^{n}(t)\|_{L^{\frac{N}{3},\infty}}\leq C\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{\frac{N}{3},\infty}}\quad\text{and}\quad\|\theta^{n}(t)\|_{L^{N,\infty}}\leq C\|\theta_{0}\|_{L^{N,\infty}}\quad\hbox{for all}\ \ t\geq 0.

Note that the above estimates are not sufficient to pass to the limit in the nonlinear terms of system (1). So we shall take advantage of the smoothing properties given by the Stokes operator in the equation for the velocity. Let qq be in ]N,∞[.]N,\infty[. Putting together Remark 3 and the embedding LN,∞↪B˙q,∞Nq−1,L^{N,\infty}\hookrightarrow\dot{B}^{\frac{N}{q}-1}_{q,\infty}, we discover that

ν​‖un‖L~t1​(B˙q,∞Nq+1)≤C⁡(‖u0‖LN,∞+‖un⊗un‖L~t1​(B˙q,∞Nq)+‖θn‖Lt1​(LN,∞)).\nu\|u^{n}\|_{\widetilde{L}^{1}_{t}(\dot{B}^{\frac{N}{q}+1}_{q,\infty})}\leq C\Bigl(\|u_{0}\|_{L^{N,\infty}}+\|u^{n}\otimes u^{n}\|_{\widetilde{L}^{1}_{t}(\dot{B}^{\frac{N}{q}}_{q,\infty})}+\|\theta^{n}\|_{L^{1}_{t}(L^{N,\infty})}\Bigr). (18)

3.2 Global existence: the general case

4 Uniqueness

Let us first give the heuristics of the proof of Theorem 3.

Consider two solutions (θ1,u1,∇Π1)(\theta_{1},u_{1},\nabla\Pi_{1}) and (θ2,u2,∇Π2)(\theta_{2},u_{2},\nabla\Pi_{2}) of system (1) corresponding to the same initial data. Assume that for some 1≤p<2​N,1\leq p<2N,

(θi,ui)∈LT∞​(B˙p,∞−1+Np)×(LT∞​(B˙p,∞−1+Np)∩L~T1​(B˙p,∞1+Np))Nfori=1,2.(\theta_{i},u_{i})\in L^{\infty}_{T}(\dot{B}^{-1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty})\times\Bigl(L^{\infty}_{T}(\dot{B}^{-1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty})\cap\widetilde{L}^{1}_{T}(\dot{B}^{1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty})\Bigr)^{N}\quad\hbox{for}\ \ i=1,2.

The system satisfied by the difference (δθ,δu,∇δΠ)(\delta\!\theta,\delta\!u,\nabla\delta\!\Pi) between the two solutions reads

{∂tδ​θ+div​(u1​δ​θ)=−div​(θ2​δ​u),∂tδu+div(u1⊗δu)−νΔδu+∇δΠ=−div(δu⊗u2)+δθeN.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\delta\!\theta+\,\mbox{div}\,(u_{1}\delta\!\theta)=-\,\mbox{div}\,(\theta_{2}\,\delta\!u),\\ \partial_{t}\delta\!u+\,\mbox{div}\,(u_{1}\otimes\delta\!u)-\nu\Delta\delta\!u+\nabla\delta\!\Pi=-\,\mbox{div}\,(\delta\!u\otimes u_{2})+\delta\!\theta\,e_{N}.\end{array}\right.

Note that the right-hand side of the first equation (which is a transport equation associated to the vector field u1u_{1}) is (at least) one derivative less regular than θ2.\theta_{2}. Because no smoothing property may be expected for such an equation, this obliges us to perform estimates in LT∞​(B˙p,∞−2+Np)L^{\infty}_{T}(\dot{B}^{-2+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty}) for δ​θ\delta\!\theta rather than in LT∞​(B˙p,∞−1+Np).L^{\infty}_{T}(\dot{B}^{-1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty}). Now, due to the coupling between the equations for δ​u\delta\!u and δ​θ,\delta\!\theta, this loss of one derivative also occurs in the estimates for δ​u.\delta\!u. This yields the constraint p<2​Np<2N when bounding the quadratic terms (see Proposition 4).

The second difficulty that we have to face is much more serious: as the space L~T1​(B˙p,∞1+Np)\widetilde{L}^{1}_{T}(\dot{B}^{1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty}) fails to be embedded in LT1​(Lip),L^{1}_{T}(\hbox{Lip}), the vector field u1u_{1} is not in LT1​(Lip).L^{1}_{T}(\hbox{Lip}). Therefore, the initial regularity of δ​θ\delta\!\theta need not be preserved during the evolution. It turns out however that B˙p,∞1+Np\dot{B}^{1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty} is embedded in the set Loglip{\rm Loglip} of Log-Lipschitz functions so that one may resort to arguments similar to those used by H. Bahouri and J.-Y. Chemin in [3] to prove estimates with (small) loss of regularity. Of course, we will have to cope with the fact that, due to the “tilde”, the space L~T1​(B˙p,∞1+Np)\widetilde{L}^{1}_{T}(\dot{B}^{1+\frac{N}{p}}_{p,\infty}) is not quite embedded in LT1​(Loglip).L^{1}_{T}({\rm Loglip}). Overcoming this ultimate difficulty is the purpose of the next subsection.

4.3 The limit case p=2​Np=2N

Carrying out the method which has been used in the previous section to the limit case p=2​Np=2N seems hopeless. Indeed, we would have to deal with the product θ2​δ​u\theta_{2}\delta\!u while θ2∈LT∞​(B˙2​N,∞−12−ε)\theta_{2}\in L^{\infty}_{T}(\dot{B}^{-\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}_{2N,\infty}) and δ​u∈L~T1​(B˙2​N,∞12−ε)\delta\!u\in\widetilde{L}^{1}_{T}(\dot{B}^{\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon}_{2N,\infty}) for some ε>0,\varepsilon>0, which does not make sense since the sum of indices of regularity is negative.

In order to meet the index p=2​N,p=2N, one may resort to Besov spaces with third index 11 so as to have a velocity field in LT1​(Lip).L^{1}_{T}(\hbox{Lip}). Thus no losing a priori estimate is needed. On the other hand, due to the weak regularity assumptions, we shall be in the limit case for product laws in Proposition 4 so that a logarithmic interpolation argument (similar to that which has been used in [8] and [10]) will be required. Let us state the result.

Theorem 5

5 Appendix

This appendix is devoted to proving the estimates for the convection terms that we used in section 4.2.

Lemma 4

Let (αq)q∈ℤ(\alpha_{q})_{q\in{\mathbb{Z}}} be a sequence of nonnegative functions over [0,T].[0,T]. Let s1,s_{1}, s2,s_{2}, pp satisfy

0≤αq′​(t)−αq​(t)≤12​(s1+s2+N​min⁡(0,1−2p))​(q′−q).0\leq\alpha_{q^{\prime}}(t)-\alpha_{q}(t)\leq\frac{1}{2}\biggl(s_{1}+s_{2}+N\min\Bigl(0,1-\frac{2}{p}\Bigr)\biggr)(q^{\prime}-q). (32)

Then for all r∈[1,∞],r\in[1,\infty], there exists a constant CC depending only on s1,s_{1}, s2,s_{2}, NN and pp such that for all function bb and solenoidal vector field aa over ℝN,\mathbb{R}^{N}, the following estimate holds true for all t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]:

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
